Repo: H:\Kasirku — a Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack) multi-tenant POS/accounting SaaS called "Kasirku", live at https://createimpact.id, using Supabase (Postgres+Auth+RLS) and Server Actions. I need a concrete implementation plan for a new initiative: an Android app for cashiers who use ONLY a tablet (no PC at all), so kitchen/bar ticket printing works without any separate local server.

## Background (already established this session, don't re-derive)

Kasirku already has a "kitchen ticket" printing pipeline:
- `src/lib/escpos.ts` — `buildKitchenTicket(input): Buffer` builds raw ESC/POS bytes for a ticket (station name, source, item list). Pure, Node-only (uses `Buffer`), no I/O.
- `src/lib/kitchen-print.ts` — `buildKitchenPrintJobs(supabase, businessId, job)` queries the `kitchen_printers` table, matches items to printers by `categories`, and for each matching printer calls `buildKitchenTicket` and returns `{printerName, address, bytesBase64}[]` (base64 so it's safe to send to the client). **It currently filters to `connection_type === "lan"` only** — bluetooth-typed rows are silently dropped (there's a test literally named "ignores bluetooth printers (LAN dispatch only)" confirming this is deliberate/current, not a bug).
- `src/app/business/[businessId]/pos/actions.ts` — `checkout()` and `updateSelfOrderStatus()` (Server Actions) call `buildKitchenPrintJobsForItems`/`buildKitchenPrintJobs` and return the jobs array as `printJobs` in their result, alongside the normal transaction result. This part runs on Vercel and never touches the actual printer — building ticket bytes is server-side and unaffected by this new work.
- `src/lib/dispatch-print-jobs.ts` (client, `"use client"`) — `dispatchPrintJobs(businessId, jobs)` loops the jobs and calls `printViaAgent` for each, collects failures, reports them via `logKitchenPrintFailures` server action. Called fire-and-forget (`void dispatchPrintJobs(...)`) from `pos-screen.tsx` (`handleConfirmPayment`, `handleOrderStatus`) and `src/hooks/use-offline-sync.ts` (offline retry path) — always AFTER the sale/status-update already succeeded, so printer failures never block a sale.
- `src/lib/print-agent-client.ts` (client) — `printViaAgent(address, bytesBase64)` does a `fetch` to `${NEXT_PUBLIC_PRINT_AGENT_URL}/print` (default `http://127.0.0.1:9123/print`) with `{ip, port, bytes}`, returns `{ok:true}` or `{ok:false, reason, error}`.
- `print-agent/` — a NEW standalone Node app (built this session) that runs on the cashier's WINDOWS PC, listens on `127.0.0.1:9123` (loopback only), and on `POST /print {ip,port,bytes}` opens a raw `net.Socket` to the printer's LAN IP and writes the bytes (`print-agent/src/printSocket.ts`'s `sendToPrinter`). Packaged as a standalone `.exe` via Node's Single Executable Application feature (`print-agent/scripts/build-exe.cjs`), installed via `print-agent/install.ps1` (copies exe to `%LOCALAPPDATA%`, adds a Windows Startup-folder shortcut, PowerShell). This solves LAN printing **only for shops with a Windows PC** — browsers can't open raw TCP sockets themselves, and Vercel's server can't reach a shop's private LAN IP, hence needing this local relay.

**The gap this new plan must close:** a shop where the cashier has ONLY an Android tablet (no PC at all) has no way to run `print-agent`, so LAN kitchen printing is impossible there, and Bluetooth kitchen printing has literally never been implemented (dead code, see above). The project owner wants a strategy like Moka POS: a downloadable Android app (NOT via Play Store — will be side-loaded via a direct APK download link, self-signed, no Google Play Developer account) where printer settings (both LAN and Bluetooth) live inside the app itself, and kitchen/bar tickets print directly from the tablet with nothing extra needed in the kitchen/bar.

**Explicitly OUT of scope:** the cashier's own receipt (struk) printing is unaffected — it already works today via a plain `window.print()` browser dialog routed to an OS-level Bluetooth print service (not implemented by Kasirku's code at all, see `src/app/business/[businessId]/(dashboard)/transactions/[transactionId]/receipt/`). Don't touch receipt printing.

**Current `kitchen_printers` table schema** (from `supabase/migrations/20260702100500_fnb_support_tables.sql`):
```
kitchen_printers: id uuid PK, business_id uuid FK, name text, categories text[] default '{}',
  connection_type text default 'bluetooth' check in ('bluetooth','lan'), address text nullable
```
`address` is free text today: for LAN it's `ip:port`, for bluetooth it's just an arbitrary device-name label (no real MAC address stored) — there's no device-picker/pairing flow anywhere, `src/app/business/[businessId]/(dashboard)/settings/add-printer-form.tsx` just has a free-text input whose placeholder changes based on connection type.

**Environment fact**: this Windows dev machine currently has ZERO Android tooling — no JDK, no Android SDK, no Gradle, no Android Studio (confirmed via a clean check). The user has approved installing JDK + Android SDK command-line tools (not full Android Studio) on this machine so builds/tests can happen directly here.

**Distribution decision (confirmed with user):** self-signed APK via direct download link, no Play Store, no Google Play Developer account needed.

## What I need from you

A concrete, actionable implementation plan covering:

1. **App architecture decision**: I'm leaning toward Capacitor (wraps the *existing* live Next.js site at createimpact.id in a native WebView via `server.url` config — NOT a static bundle, since this app is Server-Actions-heavy and not statically exportable) plus ONE custom native Capacitor plugin (Kotlin) for the two things a browser can't do: open a raw TCP socket, and talk Bluetooth Classic SPP to a thermal printer. Validate or challenge this choice — is there a better-fit approach given the constraints (existing huge Next.js app, want to reuse ~everything, minimal new native surface)? Consider alternatives (React Native, a thin custom WebView Android project without Capacitor, etc.) but only recommend switching if there's a concrete, material advantage.

2. **Native plugin design**: exact methods the plugin should expose (e.g. `printLan(ip, port, bytesBase64)`, `printBluetooth(address, bytesBase64)`, `listPairedBluetoothDevices()` returning bonded devices only — deliberately avoid active BT discovery/scanning so we can skip the location-permission requirement, since pairing happens once via Android's normal system Bluetooth settings), what Android permissions are actually required (Android 12+ `BLUETOOTH_CONNECT` vs legacy `BLUETOOTH`/`BLUETOOTH_ADMIN`), and the plan for graceful behavior on very old vs new Android versions.

3. **Web-side wiring**: how `dispatch-print-jobs.ts` should branch between "native platform available → call the plugin directly" vs "browser+PC → existing print-agent HTTP flow" (both must keep working — this is an additional deployment model, not a replacement). What changes `kitchen-print.ts` needs (removing the LAN-only filter so bluetooth jobs are built too) and what (if any) DB migration is needed so `add-printer-form.tsx` can capture a *real* Bluetooth MAC address from the native device picker instead of a free-text label, while still degrading sensibly when the same settings page is opened in a normal browser (no native plugin available).

4. **Repo layout**: where should the Capacitor project live relative to `H:\Kasirku` (e.g. a new top-level `android-app/` folder, sibling to `print-agent/`) — should NOT interfere with the Next.js app's build or the print-agent's build.

5. **Build/tooling setup steps** for this specific Windows machine: what exactly needs installing (JDK version, Android SDK components — cmdline-tools, platform-tools, a platform + build-tools version), and the concrete commands to get from zero to a debug-signed installable APK, plus how to generate a simple release keystore for a self-signed release APK suitable for direct-download distribution.

6. **Verification plan**: since there's no physical Android device/printer available for real hardware testing, what CAN be meaningfully verified (e.g. Android emulator install + WebView loads the site + login works; a Kotlin unit test or manual adb-based smoke test of the native plugin's LAN socket path against a fake TCP listener, similar to how print-agent was verified this session; Bluetooth path likely can't be verified without real hardware — say so explicitly rather than pretending otherwise).

Please produce a detailed, staged implementation plan (this is a big feature — break it into clear phases/milestones, e.g. Phase 1: scaffold Capacitor app + confirm WebView loads the live site; Phase 2: native LAN print plugin + wire to dispatch-print-jobs.ts + verify against a fake TCP printer; Phase 3: native Bluetooth plugin + device picker in settings UI; Phase 4: packaging/signing/distribution). Call out risks and unknowns honestly (e.g. Bluetooth Classic SPP compatibility varies by printer model, can't be fully verified without real hardware in this session).

# Kasirku Print Agent

Runs on the cashier's PC to relay kitchen/bar print jobs from the browser to LAN thermal
printers. Browsers can't open raw TCP sockets, and Kasirku's server (Vercel) can't reach a
printer's private LAN IP (`192.168.x.x`) either — so this small local service does it instead.

## Why this exists

The POS page (running in the cashier's browser, physically on the shop's own network) can't
talk to a printer at `192.168.1.50:9100` directly — this agent listens on `127.0.0.1:9123`
(loopback only, never reachable from the network), accepts a print job over local HTTP from the
browser, and opens the raw TCP socket to the printer on the agent's behalf, since the agent is on
the same LAN as the printer.

Previously, print dispatch ran as a Next.js Server Action on Vercel — which can never reach a
shop's private LAN IP from the cloud. That's why LAN kitchen printing has never actually worked.

---

## Instalasi di komputer kasir (untuk pemilik toko/kasir, bukan developer)

Tidak perlu install Node.js atau paham command line — cukup file `.exe` siap pakai.

1. Minta file `kasirku-print-agent.exe` beserta `install.ps1` (satu folder) dari developer.
2. Klik kanan `install.ps1` -> **Run with PowerShell**.
   - Kalau muncul peringatan biru "Windows protected your PC": klik **More info** -> **Run

# Capacitor server.url Configuration

## Primary Purpose

The `server.url` option allows you to redirect the native application to load from an external URL instead of the bundled web assets in `webDir`. As the documentation states: "Load an external URL in the Web View. This is intended for use with live-reload servers."

This capability is particularly useful during development when you want to test your app against a running development server rather than recompiling and redeploying the bundled assets each time.

## Related Configuration Options

**server.cleartext**: Controls whether unencrypted HTTP traffic is permitted in the Web View. By default, Android disables cleartext traffic (API 28+). Enabling this option is recommended when using live-reload servers that typically serve unencrypted content. The documentation notes this is "not intended for use in production."

**server.allowNavigation**: Expands the URLs the Web View can navigate to beyond the default behavior. Normally, external URLs open in an external browser rather than within the Web View. This option permits additional URLs to load internally, with an empty array as the default.

**androidScheme/iosScheme**: Configure the local protocol scheme (`https` on Android by default, `capacitor` on iOS). These schemes handle requests to your local server, though the Android documentation cautions that custom schemes may cause routing issues with modern WebView versions.

## Important Caveat

All these server-related options carry explicit warnings: they are development tools only and unsuitable for production deployments.

## 1. Architecture decision: Capacitor is the right call — validated, not just accepted

**Recommendation: keep Capacitor + one custom Kotlin plugin, using `server.url` pointing at `https://createimpact.id`.**

Why it beats the alternatives for *this specific app*:

- **React Native**: RN doesn't run your existing DOM/CSS/React-19-with-Server-Components app — RN components aren't DOM. To "reuse ~everything" you'd still embed a WebView (`react-native-webview`) inside RN, meaning you'd carry RN's whole toolchain (Metro, RN CLI, RN's own native module system) *on top of* still needing custom native code for TCP/Bluetooth — strictly more moving parts than Capacitor for zero benefit, since you're not writing any real RN-native UI. Reject.
- **Thin custom WebView Android project (no Capacitor)**: technically viable — Capacitor's Android runtime is itself thin (~a `WebView` + a bridge). But you'd be re-deriving, by hand: the JS↔Kotlin bridge (`addJavascriptInterface`/`evaluateJavascript` marshalling, promise semantics, error propagation), persistent cookie-jar setup, mixed-content/cleartext policy, Android back-button handling inside a WebView, permission-request plumbing, and a Gradle project skeleton — all things Capacitor already provides as battle-tested primitives (`registerPlugin`, `PluginCall`, `@Permission` annotations). For one plugin this is a real trade-off, not a slam dunk either way, but Capacitor's plugin API is well-documented and the incremental weight of `@capacitor/core` + `@capacitor/android` is small. Verdict: not enough concrete advantage to justify hand-rolling the bridge — stick with Capacitor.
- **Trusted Web Activity (TWA/Bubblewrap)**: works without Play Store (Digital Asset Links via a hosted `.well-known/assetlinks.json`, not a store listing) and is even lighter than Capacitor. But TWA is fundamentally a Chrome Custom Tab wrapper — there is **no supported JS↔native bridge** for arbitrary custom Kotlin code (no raw-socket, no Bluetooth SPP). Since the entire point of this app is exactly that bridge, TWA is disqualified outright, not just "worse."

**One important nuance to flag explicitly, since it affects risk posture**: Capacitor's own docs describe `server.url` as *"intended for use with live-reload servers"* and explicitly warn it's *"not intended for use in production."* That warning exists because most Capacitor apps ship bundled `webDir` assets for offline-first behavior and are also normally submitted to app-store review (where a "pure remote WebView wrapper" can draw scrutiny, especially on iOS). Neither of those reasons applies to Kasirku:
- The app is intentionally NOT going through any app store (self-signed, side-loaded APK) — no reviewer to reject a remote-URL app.
- Kasirku already accepts "online-only except a narrow POS-page service-worker cache" as its architecture (`public/sw.js` already only caches the POS route + static assets, deliberately not the rest of the dashboard) — a remote-URL wrapper is consistent with that existing risk posture, not a new one.

So this remains the correct choice for this project, but it means: (a) don't expect first-class support/examples for this exact configuration from Capacitor's docs/community, test it directly rather than trusting it by analogy, and (b) `server.allowNavigation` needs `createimpact.id` (and any auth-callback subpaths) explicitly listed so in-app navigations don't unexpectedly kick out to the system browser and lose the native bridge context.

**Auth-flow check (relevant to server.url risk)**: `src/app/login/page.tsx` uses `supabase.auth.signInWithPassword` — a plain in-page call, no external redirect, no OAuth popup, no magic-link. This is good news: the primary cashier login path never leaves the WebView. The only external-browser touchpoint is `src/app/auth/callback/route.ts`, used for password-reset/email-confirmation links opened from an email client — that's expected to open in a real browser (the user isn't inside the tablet app when they tap an email link), and is out of scope to deep-link back into the app for this initiative.

**Package versions to pin (checked live against npm as of today):** `@capacitor/core` / `@capacitor/android` / `@capacitor/cli` are all at **8.4.2**. Capacitor 8 requires **minSdkVersion 24** (matches Capacitor's own stated Android 7+ floor), **compileSdk/targetSdk 36**, **AGP 8.13.0**, **Gradle 8.14.3**, **Kotlin 2.2.20**, and **JDK 17+ (21 recommended)**.

---

## 2. Native plugin design

Single plugin, e.g. `KitchenPrinterPlugin` (Kotlin), registered on the JS side as `"KitchenPrinter"`.

### Methods

```kotlin
@PluginMethod
fun printLan(call: PluginCall)          // { ip, port, bytesBase64, timeoutMs? } -> { ok, error? }

@PluginMethod
fun printBluetooth(call: PluginCall)    // { address, bytesBase64, timeoutMs? } -> { ok, error? }

@PluginMethod
fun listPairedBluetoothDevices(call: PluginCall)  // {} -> { devices: [{ name, address }] }

@PluginMethod
fun isBluetoothEnabled(call: PluginCall) // {} -> { enabled: boolean }
```

- **`printLan`**: mirrors `print-agent/src/printSocket.ts`'s `sendToPrinter` almost 1:1 — `java.net.Socket()`, `connect(InetSocketAddress(ip, port), timeoutMs)`, write the decoded bytes, flush, close. Map exceptions to the *same error vocabulary* the existing print-agent already uses (`connect_timeout`, or the raw exception message) so `dispatch-print-jobs.ts`'s failure-reporting UI/logs read consistently regardless of which dispatch path handled the job. **Must run off the main thread** (`NetworkOnMainThreadException` otherwise) — Capacitor plugin calls already execute on a background thread pool by default, but do the I/O inside an explicit `Dispatchers.IO` coroutine anyway rather than relying on that.
- **`printBluetooth`**: `BluetoothAdapter.getDefaultAdapter().getRemoteDevice(address)` → `device.createRfcommSocketToServiceRecord(SPP_UUID)` where `SPP_UUID = "00001101-0000-1000-8000-00805F9B34FB"` (the standard Serial Port Profile UUID essentially every cheap ESC/POS Bluetooth thermal printer uses) → `bluetoothAdapter.cancelDiscovery()` (cheap, recommended even when not scanning — avoids flaky/slow connects) → `socket.connect()` (blocking, off-main-thread) → write bytes to `socket.outputStream` → close. **Known real-world variance to design for**: some printer BT stacks reject the secure RFCOMM socket and only work with `createInsecureRfcommSocketToServiceRecord` — implement secure-first with an automatic insecure-socket fallback on `IOException`, and say explicitly (see §6) this can't be fully validated without real hardware.
- **`listPairedBluetoothDevices`**: reads `bluetoothAdapter.bondedDevices` only — **deliberately never calls `startDiscovery()`**. This is the load-bearing design choice that avoids `ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION` entirely: Android only requires location permission for *active* BT scanning, not for reading devices already paired via system Settings. Matches the intended UX exactly: cashier pairs the printer once in Android's own Bluetooth settings, then Kasirku's picker just lists what's already bonded.
- **`isBluetoothEnabled`**: `bluetoothAdapter?.isEnabled ?: false` — drives a "turn on Bluetooth first" hint in the settings UI. Also guard the case `BluetoothAdapter.getDefaultAdapter()` returns `null` (tablet has no BT radio at all) → return a structured `{ enabled: false, supported: false }` rather than throwing.

### Permissions

```xml
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.BLUETOOTH" android:maxSdkVersion="30" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.BLUETOOTH_ADMIN" android:maxSdkVersion="30" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.BLUETOOTH_CONNECT" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />
```

- API ≤30: `BLUETOOTH`/`BLUETOOTH_ADMIN` are install-time "normal" permissions — no runtime prompt.
- API 31+ (Android 12+): `BLUETOOTH_CONNECT` is a runtime-dangerous permission required for `createRfcommSocketToServiceRecord`/`connect()`. Request it via Capacitor's `@Permission`/`requestPermissionForAlias` pattern the first time a BT method is called, branching on `Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.S`.
- **We never request `BLUETOOTH_SCAN` or any `ACCESS_*_LOCATION` permission at all**, because we never call `startDiscovery()`. Worth stating to the user explicitly: this is a genuinely better cashier UX than most POS apps get (no scary location-permission dialog on install), and it's a direct consequence of the "bonded devices only" design.
- `INTERNET` is already implicitly required for the WebView to load the site at all — no prompt, install-time only.

### Old vs new Android behavior

- `minSdkVersion 24` matches Capacitor 8's floor — no meaningful population below that on tablets bought for this purpose today.
- `targetSdkVersion 36` is what triggers Android's *behavioral* enforcement of the split legacy/modern BT permission model — this applies based on the app's targetSdk regardless of Play Store distribution, so the manifest above is required correctness, not just best practice.

---

## 3. Web-side wiring

### A structural point that has to be decided up front

Because we're using `server.url` (not a bundled `webDir`), the JS that runs inside the WebView **is the exact same bundle Vercel serves to regular browsers**. That means `@capacitor/core` and the plugin's JS wrapper must live in the **main Kasirku Next.js app** (`H:\Kasirku\package.json`, `src/lib/`), not just inside the new Android project — the Android project supplies only the native Gradle/Kotlin side (`@capacitor/android` + the plugin's Kotlin source). `@capacitor/core` is designed for exactly this (small, tree-shakes to near-nothing, no-ops safely on regular browsers via `Capacitor.isNativePlatform()` returning `false`).

New file `src/lib/kitchen-printer-plugin.ts`:

```ts
import { registerPlugin } from "@capacitor/core";

export interface KitchenPrinterPlugin {
  printLan(opts: { ip: string; port: number; bytesBase64: string }): Promise<{ ok: boolean; error?: string }>;
  printBluetooth(opts: { address: string; bytesBase64: string }): Promise<{ ok: boolean; error?: string }>;
  listPairedBluetoothDevices(): Promise<{ devices: { name: string; address: string }[] }>;
  isBluetoothEnabled(): Promise<{ enabled: boolean; supported: boolean }>;
}

export default registerPlugin<KitchenPrinterPlugin>("KitchenPrinter");
```

### `kitchen-print.ts` — remove the LAN-only filter, and carry `connectionType`

Currently `buildKitchenPrintJobs` filters to `connection_type === "lan"` and the payload has no field telling the client which transport to use. Once bluetooth jobs are built too, the client **must** know which transport each job needs — today's ambiguity ("is `address` an `ip:port` or a device label?") only worked because bluetooth was filtered out entirely. Required change:

```ts
export type KitchenPrintJobPayload = {
  printerName: string;
  address: string;
  connectionType: "lan" | "bluetooth";
  bytesBase64: string;
};
// ...
const printersWithAddress = (printers ?? []).filter((p) => !!p.address); // both types now
// ... map(({ printer, items }) => ({ ..., connectionType: printer.connection_type, ... }))
```

This also **breaks and requires updating** `src/lib/kitchen-print.test.ts`'s `"ignores bluetooth printers (LAN dispatch only)"` test — its current assertion (`jobs` is empty for a bluetooth-only printer) becomes actively wrong once the filter is removed; the test suite will fail loudly rather than silently regress, which is the right failure mode, but the test needs to be rewritten as part of this change, not just left broken.

### `dispatch-print-jobs.ts` — three-way branch, not two

The subtlety here: on a plain-browser (PC + print-agent) path, `dispatch-print-jobs.ts` will now also receive bluetooth jobs (since `kitchen-print.ts` no longer filters them server-side). Sending a MAC-address string into `print-agent-client.ts`'s `printViaAgent` (which does `address.split(":")` expecting `ip:port`) would silently attempt a nonsensical connect and produce a confusing error. So the real branching is per-job, not just native-vs-web:

```ts
import { Capacitor } from "@capacitor/core";
import KitchenPrinter from "./kitchen-printer-plugin";

async function dispatchOne(job: KitchenPrintJobPayload): Promise<PrintAgentResult> {
  if (Capacitor.isNativePlatform()) {
    const result =
      job.connectionType === "lan"
        ? await KitchenPrinter.printLan({ ...parseIpPort(job.address), bytesBase64: job.bytesBase64 })
        : await KitchenPrinter.printBluetooth({ address: job.address, bytesBase64: job.bytesBase64 });
    return result.ok ? { ok: true } : { ok: false, reason: "printer_unreachable", error: result.error ?? "unknown_error" };
  }
  if (job.connectionType === "bluetooth") {
    return { ok: false, reason: "printer_unreachable", error: "unsupported_on_web" }; // no network call at all
  }
  return printViaAgent(job.address, job.bytesBase64); // existing PC + print-agent path, unchanged
}
```

Both deployment models keep working simultaneously, exactly as required — `printViaAgent`/`print-agent-client.ts`/`print-agent/` are untouched.

### DB migration and settings UI

The `kitchen_printers.address` column can already hold a real MAC address (`connection_type`/`address` already distinguish transport) — **no schema change is strictly required for storage**. But today `address` for bluetooth doubles as a human-friendly label (e.g. `"KITCHEN-80"`); once the native picker fills it with a real MAC (`AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF`), the printer list in `settings/page.tsx` (`{p.address ? \` · ${p.address}\` : ""}` at line ~202) would show an unfriendly MAC instead. Recommend one small additive, backward-compatible migration:

```sql
-- supabase/migrations/<timestamp>_kitchen_printers_device_label.sql
alter table public.kitchen_printers add column device_label text;
```

Nullable, no backfill needed (existing rows just render as they do today). Then:
- `settings/actions.ts`'s `addKitchenPrinter` reads an extra optional `deviceLabel` field and inserts `device_label: deviceLabel || null`.
- `settings/page.tsx`'s select adds `device_label` and the render becomes `p.address ? \` · ${p.device_label ?? p.address}\` : ""`.
- `add-printer-form.tsx`: when `connectionType === "bluetooth"` **and** `Capacitor.isNativePlatform()`, swap the free-text input for a "Pilih dari perangkat Bluetooth yang sudah dipasangkan" picker driven by `KitchenPrinter.listPairedBluetoothDevices()`, filling hidden `address` (MAC) and `deviceLabel` (friendly name) inputs on selection, submitted through the same existing server action — no action *signature* change, just one more form field. When BT is off, surface `isBluetoothEnabled()` as a hint. **On a normal browser** (no native plugin — including on a PC opening the same settings page), the form falls back to exactly today's free-text input, unchanged — degrades sensibly as required. The LAN input path is untouched either way (no LAN auto-discovery is being built — out of scope, not requested).
